context: Both diagrams have vertices 1 through 5 and the same seven undirected edges, all listed below. The unweighted graph on the left, labeled “All edges are equivalent,” has no numerical labels. The weighted graph on the right, labeled “Edges have weights,” shows a decimal number beside each edge.
description: “All edges are equivalent” means that existing edges do not differ in strength or length. It does not mean every pair of vertices is connected. The weights on the right range from 0.2 to 1.0, with no physical unit specified. Each row of the table gives an edge's weight and location as shown in the figure.

frames.explanation: Adding weights leaves the vertices and their connections unchanged. Depending on the application, weights can represent distance, cost, or closeness and can be used to compute shortest paths or minimum spanning trees.
frames.title: Unweighted and weighted graphs: assigning numerical weights to edges

summary: Adding numerical weights to the same connections illustrates the difference between unweighted and weighted graphs.

tables.caption: Edge weights in the undirected graph on the right
